title: Words for Thinkers
sub: Vocabulary for reading and discussing big ideas.

cards.def: The defining spirit or mood of a particular period.
examples: The film captured the zeitgeist of the 1960s.
Social media shapes the zeitgeist of our time.
The novel perfectly reflects the zeitgeist of post-independence India.
Good advertisers try to capture the zeitgeist.

cards.def: Excessive pride or self-confidence, often leading to downfall.
examples: His hubris led him to ignore every warning.
The general's hubris cost him the battle.
It was hubris to launch without any testing.
Greek tragedies often show heroes destroyed by hubris.

cards.def: A method of reaching truth through the clash of opposing ideas.
examples: Socrates taught through dialectic.
The professor used dialectic to help students question their beliefs.
Hegel's dialectic moves from thesis to antithesis to synthesis.
Their debate was a lively dialectic between two views.

cards.def: A quality that evokes pity or sadness.
examples: The novel's pathos left readers in tears.
The film's final scene was full of pathos.
The speaker used pathos to win the audience's sympathy.
There is real pathos in the old man's letters.

cards.def: The characteristic spirit or guiding beliefs of a culture or group.
examples: The company's ethos is radical transparency.
The school's ethos values kindness over marks.
Teamwork is part of our company ethos.
The startup's ethos is to move fast and learn.

cards.def: Persuasion through logic and reason.
examples: Her speech relied on logos, citing data.
Lawyers use logos when they present evidence step by step.
Her essay was strong on logos but weak on emotion.
Ads often mix logos with emotional appeal.

cards.def: The branch of philosophy concerned with the nature and limits of knowledge.
examples: Epistemology asks how we can know what we know.
The philosophy course starts with epistemology.
Epistemology asks whether our senses can be trusted.
Science raises many questions of epistemology.

cards.def: The branch of philosophy concerned with the nature of being.
examples: Ontology debates whether numbers really exist.
Ontology asks what kinds of things really exist.
The lecture on ontology left me thinking about the nature of time.
In philosophy class, we compared Indian and Western ontology.

cards.def: The ethical view that the best action maximizes overall happiness.
examples: Utilitarianism judges a policy by its outcomes.
Under utilitarianism, saving five lives is better than saving one.
Critics say utilitarianism can ignore individual rights.
The government used utilitarianism to justify the new highway.

cards.def: A philosophy of calm acceptance of what cannot be controlled.
examples: Stoicism taught him to stay steady in a crisis.
Reading about Stoicism helped me handle stress at work.
Stoicism teaches us to focus on what we can control.
Marcus Aurelius is a famous voice of Stoicism.

cards.def: A focus on practical consequences over abstract theory.
examples: Her pragmatism got the deal done.
Pragmatism helped the leaders reach a quick agreement.
He chose pragmatism over perfection and shipped the product.
American pragmatism values ideas that work in practice.

cards.def: Relating to human existence and the search for meaning.
examples: He faced an existential crisis at forty.
Climate change is an existential threat to island nations.
The film explores existential questions about life and death.
After retiring, he felt an existential emptiness.

cards.def: A typical model or framework of thinking in a field.
examples: Darwin's work shifted the paradigm of biology.
The internet created a new paradigm for business.
Einstein's theory changed the paradigm of physics.
We need a new paradigm for teaching languages.

cards.def: Something placed in the wrong historical period.
examples: A wristwatch in a Roman film is an anachronism.
Typewriters now seem like an anachronism.
The historian spotted an anachronism in the costume.
Some old laws are an anachronism in modern society.

cards.def: The middle class, especially as owners of property and capital.
examples: Marx wrote about the bourgeoisie and the proletariat.
The novel mocks the comfortable life of the bourgeoisie.
The French Revolution changed the power of the bourgeoisie.
In the story, the bourgeoisie live in big city houses.

cards.def: The working class, especially industrial workers.
examples: The proletariat organized into unions.
The proletariat worked long hours in the mills.
Communist leaders spoke for the proletariat.
The play shows the struggles of the urban proletariat.

cards.def: A medieval system of land held in exchange for service.
examples: Feudalism bound peasants to the lord's estate.
Under feudalism, peasants worked the lord's land.
Feudalism declined as towns and trade grew.
The museum explains how feudalism worked in medieval Europe.

cards.def: A revival of art and learning; especially Europe's 14th–17th century rebirth.
examples: The Renaissance produced da Vinci and Michelangelo.
The Renaissance began in Italy.
Many great paintings come from the Renaissance.
Bengal saw a cultural renaissance in the nineteenth century.

cards.def: A story whose characters and events stand for deeper meanings.
examples: Animal Farm is an allegory of the Russian Revolution.
The Panchatantra stories work as allegory for human behaviour.
The film is an allegory about power and greed.
Students wrote essays on the allegory in the poem.

cards.def: A contrast between what is expected and what actually happens or is said.
examples: The fire station burned down — what irony.
The irony is that the safety officer had an accident.
She said nice weather with irony as the rain poured.
There's a sad irony in a doctor who never rests.

cards.def: A body of works regarded as authoritative or essential.
examples: Shakespeare sits at the center of the Western canon.
Tagore's poems are part of the Indian literary canon.
The course covers the canon of classic English novels.
Critics argue the canon should include more women writers.

cards.def: The art of effective or persuasive speaking and writing.
examples: Her rhetoric moved the whole crowd.
The politician's rhetoric promised more than he delivered.
Students learned rhetoric to improve their debating skills.
Empty rhetoric won't solve the water crisis.

cards.def: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something.
examples: He felt ambivalence about leaving home.
She felt ambivalence about the promotion and the extra travel.
There's public ambivalence about the new policy.
His ambivalence showed in his slow reply.

cards.def: A distrustful belief that people act only out of self-interest.
examples: Years of politics bred his cynicism.
His cynicism made it hard to trust any new manager.
Don't let cynicism stop you from trying.
Public cynicism about politicians is growing.

cards.def: A questioning attitude toward claims presented as fact.
examples: Healthy skepticism protects against misinformation.
Treat miracle health claims with skepticism.
Scientists showed skepticism about the new study.
Her skepticism helped the team avoid a bad deal.

cards.def: An imagined perfect society.
examples: Thomas More coined 'utopia' in 1516.
The new township was advertised as a utopia.
No society can become a perfect utopia.
The novel describes a utopia without money.

cards.def: An imagined society where life is miserable and oppressive.
examples: 1984 is the classic dystopia.
The film shows a dystopia controlled by machines.
Some fear social media could create a dystopia of surveillance.
Students read a dystopia novel for their English class.

cards.def: The view that only one's own mind is certain to exist.
examples: Pure solipsism is hard to argue against and impossible to live by.
Solipsism is a popular topic in first-year philosophy classes.
Taken to extremes, solipsism means doubting everyone else's mind.
The character's solipsism made him ignore other people's feelings.

cards.def: Emotional release through art or expression.
examples: The tragedy offered the audience catharsis.
Crying at the film gave me a sense of catharsis.
Writing in a journal can bring catharsis.
The match win was a catharsis for fans after years of losses.
